summary: Defines a new SMTP reply code, 521, which a host can use to say that it does not accept incoming mail. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A sign on the door: we don't take deliveries here.

questions: how does a host say it does not accept mail
subtitle: A new SMTP reply code that lets a host say plainly that it does not take mail.

tldr.problem: Mail misaddressed to hosts that run no SMTP server must be queued as a temporary error, so it sits for days before coming back with a confusing message.
tldr.mechanism: A host or an MX relay answers with the new SMTP reply code 521, meaning the host does not accept mail, and clients then return the mail or try another MX host.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Experimental and is listed as updated by RFC 7504.

today: RFC 1846 is Experimental and is updated by RFC 7504. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a 521 Reply Is Needed
sections.content:
More and more Internet hosts are dedicated to tasks such as serving NTP or DNS, and they often provide no mail service and run no SMTP server. Users sometimes misaddress mail to them.

A regular SMTP client must treat the missing server as a temporary error and queue the mail in case a server starts later. The mail then stays queued for days until it comes back with what is usually a confusing error message. This memo defines reply code 521 to say that a host does not accept incoming mail.
sections.eli5: If you mail a letter to a house nobody lives in, the post office keeps trying for days. A clear sign would save everyone the wait.

sections.title: Two Complementary Solutions
sections.content:
Two solutions MAY be implemented, and the choice is site dependent. In the first, MX relays bounce mail for the mailless host with a 521 reply during the SMTP dialog, at the RCPT TO step. If an MX relay of precedence n does this, any relay of lower precedence number for that host SHOULD do the same.

In the second, the mailless host runs a minimal SMTP server whose initial greeting is 521, with its official name or IP address as the first word after the code. The server MUST then either close the connection or answer every command except QUIT with 521, timing out if the client does not quit (5 minutes is suggested).
sections.eli5: Either a helper office takes the mail and says the house takes no mail, or the house answers the door itself and says so.

sections.title: Rules for Servers and Clients
sections.content:
A host that sends a 521 greeting MUST NOT be listed as an MX record for any domain, and it is not subject to the postmaster requirement of STD 3, RFC 1123, since a host without mail needs no one to report mail errors to.

Closing the connection right after the greeting makes some existing clients treat it as transient and requeue the mail, while leaving it open makes them send QUIT and return the mail. A client that meets a 521 greeting from an MX host must either try a different MX host or return the mail with a non-delivery report. A 521 anywhere else in the dialog MUST lead to the mail being returned.
sections.eli5: A no-mail house must not be listed as a place to send mail, and anyone who is told no must either try another address or give the letter back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo argues that running no SMTP server, or one that only emits fixed strings, should give significantly fewer opportunities for security problems than a complete SMTP implementation. Implementers are asked to report their experience to a mailing list named in the memo.
sections.eli5: A door that only ever says one sentence is harder to trick than a door that does many things.
